segments.description: Introducing Wayne Elderton, one of Canada's most respected coaching educators and a national expert on game-based coaching. Wayne has created much of the Canadian certification curriculum and has been recognised with numerous coaching awards. In his presentation, Exploring Offence and Defence, Wayne will share his expertise in creating effective and engagement player development strategies to get out of these situations or put our players into these situations. Please welcome Wayne. Canada. I'm currently the tennis director at the North Vancouver Tennis Centre. For many years I was the head course facilitator for Tennis Canada Coaching Certification in the province of British Columbia. This presentation will build on the theme of the power of play and we'll look at how we can organise point play to make better players. The theme of the presentation will be specifically about tactical development and exploring the concepts of offense and defence. I would like to thank Tennis Australia for giving me the opportunity to present at this year's coaching conference. This presentation will be split into two parts. Firstly, we will cover some theory to introduce some key concepts in tactical development. Second, we'll see a video example of a point play progression that we can use to introduce offense and defence when in a both back situation at the baseline. The players in the video are tournament players who have just made the transition from orange to green and are seeing how to utilise the bigger court space.

In my many years of certifying and observing coaches, I've found that when it comes to tactics, many coaches don't have a solid framework to build their tactics on. Coaches typically have a defined technical framework, but when it comes to tactics, they just have random tactical concepts floating around in their heads, disconnected to anything else, and especially no connection to their technical coaching. To make our coaching more effective, we need to organise and connect our tactical coaching with our technical coaching in a systematic way. In our Canadian system, we use a tactics first approach, since technique really only exists to implement tactics. Now, I want to emphasize here that I am not saying that technique is unimportant in any way. It's just that functional technical development is driven by tactics. What is most effective is integrated tactical technical training. I'd like to share two key elements that can help organise your tactical coaching. All tactical development can fit into an overall tactical mission. Now, here's what I think the mission is for all tennis tactics. Let's go through each element to solve problems, because tennis is a problem-solving challenge, by managing space and time. Now, this is fundamental not just for tennis, but for all game sports. To establish your timing, tennis is an impact sport and hinges on what happens during the contact of the ball.

And break your opponent's timing, which is what you're trying to do to them to gain points. I will often remind my coaches during their sessions, are you fulfilling the tactical mission? Having this tactical mission forefront in your mind as a coach keeps the priorities of your sessions on track, and it helps to not get caught up in disconnected or isolated technical coaching. You will see the elements of this tactical mission referenced when we watch the video example. When we apply the tactical mission to specific situations, we can also add a concept most coaches are familiar with, which is neutral, offense and defense. These are called the phases of play in our tactical system. The definition of what a phase of play is, is there an interpretation of the difficulty of the ball received? Is it producing a high, a medium or a lower challenge? And the challenge required to send a response? Is the player choosing a simpler, easier shot or a more challenging one to perform? I call it giving the knot to tennis tactics. Let's look at each one. The end stands for neutral. This is the phase where the player doesn't have the advantage, but neither does the opponent. It's a medium difficulty reception and a medium risk projection. In a neutral phase, the players aren't typically not exactly equal. A player is either slightly challenged, in which case they're trying to equalize with their shot and get back to fully neutral,

or they may have a slight advantage, in which case they could slightly increase the pressure. The O stands for offense, and this is when the reception is less difficult, so the player can safely go for a shot that is more challenging to produce. The ways a player can challenge the opponent to gain the advantage, and sometimes even finish the point, is through power, and this is where the player can increase the ball speed and basically hit a harder shot. Through precision, the player can be more accurate with their shot to make the opponent's move, for example, or time, the player can take away the opponent's time, for example, taking the ball on the rise. D stands for defense, and is when the reception is difficult, and the player must return the ball with more safety to fend off the attack. Defense includes the subcategories of staying in, so the player is just surviving, just surviving the shot and getting one more ball back into play. Or they're trying to neutralize, they're defending well enough to get back to an equal footing, to get back to neutral. Or they can counter, where the player is actually turning the tables on the opponent. For example, a solid return off a hard serve is a counter. When we look at exploring offense and defense, these are some of the tactical nuances that if coaches are aware of, they can actually help their players quite a bit. Now let's look at part two.
